newsitem.title: USA: Iowa racetrack could be worth $294 mln, study says.
newsitem.headline: Iowa racetrack could be worth $294 mln, study says.

text.p: A Polk County-owned racetrack could be worth as much as $294 million to a private operator that likely would more than double the number of slot machines at the facility, an economic impact study released Wednesday reported.

Polk County supervisors are considering selling the highly profitable and partly bond-financed Prairie Meadows Race Track to private developers and received a $200 million offer shortly after announcing its appraised value of $160 million in May.

Prairie Meadows had been on the verge of bankruptcy until the installation of slot machines in 1995 transformed it into a profit-making venture for the county. The track now has 1,100 slot machines and supervisors are considering adding 400 in 1998.

A private operation would have as many as 2,500 slot machines, bringing the cash value including capital expansion costs to about $294 million, however, the study prepared by Indiana University's Center for Urban Policy and the Environment anticipates.
Supervisors can expect competitive bids to exceed $200 million based on plans for casino expansion, the study contends.

Selling the track would ensure a fiscal return for the community and protect taxpayers from the uncertain future of gaming, but an expanded casino could also increase negative social costs, the study said.
Sale proceeds would benefit the local economy, but casino profits would likely leave the local economy also, the study said.
Prairie Meadows draws primarily from a local market and a new hotel or restaurants would divert patrons from existing facilities rather than generate new business, the study added.

Supervisors project a $16.8 million fiscal 1998 profit from the facility and have adopted plans to share 65 percent of the profits with local public schools and use 35 percent on human services needs.
Polk County has asked the state appeals board for an advisory opinion on the possible impact of receiving a profit twice the size of the county's annual budget.
Supervisors anticipate receiving the appeals board finding in about a month and will decide shortly thereafter whether they will put the track up for sale, county spokesman Phil Roeder said.
Polk County had supported the racetrack with $26.5 million of gaming revenue bonds in 1995 and $38.8 million of tax-exempt general obligation bonds in 1993 before the economic turnaround.
